title: SEBI - 0153/2003 — Fortuna Agro Plantations Ltd & Others v. Securities and Exchange Board of India
text:
IN THE SECURITIES APPELLATE TRIBUNAL
MUMBAI
Appeal No.153 of 2003
Fortuna Agro Plantations Ltd.
Bijay Kumar Agarwal
Damodar Prasad Toshniwal
Yashwant Chaudhury
Anup Kumar Agarwal
Madhu Agarwal
Anju Agarwal
Ganesh Gopal
Ashok Chatterjee
S.N. Ghoshal
Nirmalendu Guha ...... Appellants
Versus
Securities and Exchange Board of India ..…Respondent
Shri Zubin Behramkaurdin, Advocate for the Appellant
Shri Subhash Jha, Advocate for the Respondent
CORAM
Justice N.K. Sodhi, Presiding Officer
R.N. Bhardwaj, Member
Per: Justice N.K. Sodhi, Presiding Officer (Oral)
The appellant has been operating a collective investment scheme prior to
the coming into force of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Collective
Investment Schemes) Regulations, 1999 (for short “the Regulations”).
Regulation 5 of the Regulations requires that any person who immediately prior
to the commencement of the Regulations was operating a scheme, shall make an
application to the Securities and Exchange Board of India (hereinafter called “the
Board”) for the grant of a certificate within a period of two months from the date
of notification of the Regulations. An existing scheme which satisfies the Board

.2.
that the requirements specified in Regulation 9 and the conditions specified under
Regulation 71 had been fulfilled could be granted a certificate of registration
under Regulation 10 and it is only thereafter that an existing scheme could be
allowed to float new scheme on such terms and conditions as the Board may
specify. Regulation 73 of the Regulations provides that an existing collective
scheme which fails to make an application for registration or has not been grated
provisional registration or having obtained provisional registration fails to comply
with the provisions of Regulation 71 shall be wound up. The Regulation provides
for the mode and manner in which an existing scheme has then to be wound up.
Such a scheme which is to be wound up is required to send an information
memorandum to the investors who have subscribed to the scheme(s) within two
months from the date of receipt of intimation from the Board detailing the state of
affairs of the scheme, the amount repayable to each investors and the manner in
which such amount is determined. The information memorandum has then to be
send to the investors within one week from the date of its preparation and it must
explicitly state that investors desirous of continuing with the scheme shall have to
give a positive consent within one month from the date of the information
memorandum and continue with the scheme and the investors who give their
positive consent shall continue with the scheme at their own risk and
responsibility. If the positive consent to continue with the scheme is received
from only twenty five percent or less of the total number of existing investors the
scheme shall be wound up. The Regulations then provide that payment shall be
made to the investors within three months of the date the information
memorandum. An existing collective investment scheme which is not desirous of
obtaining provisional registration from the Board has to formulate a scheme of
repayment and make such repayment to the existing investors in the manner
specified in Regulation 73.

.3.
Appellant no. 1 which is a company incorporated under the Companies Act
had been operating an existing scheme and it applied for the grant of provisional
registration to the Board on 14.12.1999. It appears that the details submitted by
the appellant were found to be inadequate and that certain further
information/clarifications were sought by the Board and several other
informations were also sought in order to process the said application. Despite
several opportunity been granted to the appellant including an opportunity of
personal hearing before the then chairman the appellant did not submit the
required document/information and failed to submit the clarifications sought by
the Board. The Board by its order dated July 24, 2002 rejected the application for
registration and communicated the said order on the following day i.e. on July 24,
2002. The appellant felt aggrieved by this order and has challenged the same in
the present appeal. However, at the time of arguments the learned counsel for the
appellant did not press the challenge to this order and therefore it is not necessary
for us to deal with the objections raised in the grounds of appeal. Since the
request of the appellant for grant of provisional registration of the exiting
collective investment scheme had been turned down, the scheme had to be wound
up in terms of Regulation 73 of the Regulations. The intimation regarding the
rejection of its request for registration was received by the appellant on July 25,
2002. It was required to send an information memorandum to the investors
within two months from this date requiring them to explicitly state that those who
were desirous of continuing with the scheme should give a positive consent
within one month from the date of information memorandum so that they could
continue with the scheme. Instead of sending this information memorandum
within two months the same is alleged to have been sent on April 1, 2003. The
learned counsel for the appellant informs us that in pursuance to this
memorandum 43.76% of the investors had given their positive consent to
continue with the scheme whereas 40.38% wanted to convert their investment

.4.
into equity of the appellant company. Another 16.55% of the investors did not
respond. The memorandum contained a clause that in case any investors did not
respond, his consent would be presumed. This clause obviously runs counter to
the Regulation 73 of the Regulations but, nevertheless, some of the investors may
not have responded on the assumption that the appellant company will presume
their consent to continue with the scheme which could not be sought in the light
of the Regulations. The Board noticed this plea of the appellant in the impugned
order but did not comment on the same nor did it go into the validity of the
information memorandum presumably because by its order dated April 2, 2003 it
had already directed the appellant to refund the money collected under the scheme
to the investors within a period of one month from the date of the order following
which some action was to be initiated against it (the appellant). The appellant did
not refund the amount as directed by the Board and the latter by its order dated
August 28, 2003 debarred the appellant company, its promoters, directors and
others associated with it from operating in the capital market and from accessing
the same for a period of five years from the date of this order. It is against the
orders dated 24.7.2002, 2.4.2003, and 28.8.2003 that the present appeal has been
filed under section 15T of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (for short
“the Act”).
We have heard the learned counsel for the parties and find that on receipt
of the intimation from the Board that its application for grant of provisional
registration had been rejected the appellant did not prepare and send an
information memorandum to its investors within two months from the date of
receipt of intimation from the Board as required by Regulation 73. The
explanation furnished for this is that the business premises had been sealed by the
Calcutta Police in connection with some criminal case and that all its records had
been seized on 7.12.2001. It is common case of the parties that the premises were
unlocked and the keys were handed over to its representatives on 30.12.2002 but

.5.
according to the appellant the records which had already been seized had not been
handed over. These records were given back to the appellant thereafter and it is
for this reason that the information memorandum was prepared on 1st April, 2003
and then sent to the investors. It is true that there is a delay on the part of the
appellant in sending this information memorandum and its investors but the delay
has been satisfactorily explained by the appellant for reasons which were beyond
its control. Had it been only for the delay we would have directed the Board to
allow the appellant to proceed in accordance with the wishes of the investors after
verifying the facts in this regard. But we cannot issue such a direction because
the validity of the information memorandum had at no stage been examined by
the Board. Admittedly, the appellant did not furnish the draft of the information
memorandum after 25th July, 2002 to the Board for vetting and therefore the
question of the Board requiring the appellant to make adequate disclosures in the
said information memorandum did not arise. We are at this stage more concerned
with the rights and interest of the investors who are more than 4000 in number. If
the appellant is right that in pursuance of its information memorandum 43.76% of
its investors had given their positive concern then to require the appellant to
windup the scheme would be unfair to them. 40.38 % of the investors, according
to the appellant have already converted their investment in the equity of the
company if that is so, then they have been repaid their amounts because
conversion of their investment into equity was a mode of repayment. These facts
are now being stated before us and they had also been pleaded before the Board
but as already observed the Board has not commented at the correctness of these
assertions. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case and keeping
in view the interest of the large number of investors of the appellant we direct that
the appellant shall now furnish a fresh information memorandum and submit a
draft thereof to the Board in terms of the Regulation 73 and the Board may
require the appellant to make such other disclosures as it may deem necessary

.6.
where upon the further procedure for winding up the scheme as contemplated by
Regulation 73 shall be followed. Needless to mention that each investor shall be
given a fresh option to be exercised in terms of these Regulations. Since the
process of allowing the investor to exercise the option is to start afresh the
impugned orders dated 2.4.2003 and 28.8.2003 are set aside. Regulation 73 of the
Regulations shall now operate.
The appeal stands disposed of as above with no order as to costs.
